periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem and Thinking About It

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.5): answer three questions about sharing crayons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively, then invites the class to read along in a second pass, pointing to colour words as they appear. This unhurried encounter lets every student hear the poem's rhythm and register its two stanzas before any question is posed.
Students read the poem aloud individually or in pairs, tracking the colour words. Teacher circulates, gently correcting pronunciation of tricky words such as 'purple' and 'crayon'.

Let us think — A ("answer three questions about sharing crayons"): teacher reads each question aloud, pauses for students to think, then takes oral responses before students write their answers in the space provided.

Quick whole-class sharing of written answers; teacher writes a model sentence for one answer on the board so students can self-check. Class ends with a brisk choral re-reading of the poem's final couplet.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem hinges on the contrast 'you have / I have', which resolves when the children share — help students feel that contrast in their voices during read-aloud. Students often conflate the two characters into one; a quick 'who is speaking here?' prompt during the second reading prevents that confusion.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.5): share-and-discuss questions about crayons and drawing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by leading a quick choral recitation of the poem, using it as a warm-up to activate the colour vocabulary the class worked with earlier. No individual performance pressure — this is a shared voice-warming exercise.

Let us think — B ("share-and-discuss questions about crayons and drawing"): teacher facilitates guided conversation using the three prompts — what students share with friends, what they would draw with only three colours, and what they would draw with a fuller set. Students speak in pairs first, then share aloud with the class.

Let us speak — B ("read the colour of the ink, not the word"): teacher demonstrates the colour-word task aloud with one example, then the class attempts each word in the grid in turn. The challenge of separating word meaning from ink colour generates laughter and lively participation.

Open class debrief: teacher asks students which colour word was hardest to override and why. A few volunteers share, practising the metalinguistic idea that seeing a word and reading its colour are two different things.

periods.teacher_notes: The colour-ink task in 'Let us speak — B' is cognitively surprising for Grade III students — it helps to model it calmly and let students laugh at themselves when they slip. The 'talk in pairs' structure in the first set of prompts gives quieter students a low-stakes rehearsal before the whole-class share.

periods.activity_title: Consonant Clusters, Action Words and Alphabetical Order

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — A (p.6): consonant-cluster blend-and-say drill for gr, cr, dr, pr.
Let us learn — A (p.7): circle action words from a mixed word list.

homework.task_brief: Alphabetical order (p.13): write YELLOW, BLUE, PURPLE, GREEN, RED in alphabetical order.

time_bands.activity: Let us speak — A ("consonant-cluster blend-and-say drill for gr, cr, dr, pr"): teacher writes each cluster on the board and models the blended sound, then lists the five words for each cluster. Students repeat each set chorally, and volunteers form and say an original sentence using one word from each cluster.

Let us learn — A ("circle action words from a mixed word list"): teacher explains that action words name what someone does, then reads the twenty-word list aloud while students listen. Students then work individually to circle the action words, and pairs compare their choices before a class reveal.
Let us learn — B ("find action words in the letter grid"): teacher names each hidden word aloud; students search and circle in their textbooks. A brief class check confirms all eight words are found.

Teacher introduces the homework task — writing five colour words in alphabetical order — by demonstrating on the board what alphabetical order means using two example words. Students note the task in their exercise books.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage frequently include noun words such as 'potato' or 'sun' as action words because they sound active to them — a brief contrast of 'something you do' versus 'something that exists' helps. The consonant-cluster drill is most effective when teacher exaggerates the initial blend slightly so students feel the two sounds fuse into one. Unanchored in this sitting: the alphabet sentences (Let us learn — C) and the anagram task (item 4) — both are suitable for independent reading or a self-study moment.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p.14): match word pairs to form compound words using picture clues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking students to call out colour words from the poem and any new words they remember from working with consonant clusters, connecting the language play of this sitting to what the chapter has built. This quick oral warm-up reactivates vocabulary without requiring any previous artefact.

Teacher introduces the concept of compound words using the analogy the textbook itself uses: 'words have friends too.' Teacher demonstrates the worked example (news + bow = rainbow) on the board, explaining how two smaller words combine to make one new word.

Let us do ("match word pairs to form compound words using picture clues"): students work through the four remaining pairs — rain+paper, blue+ball, basket+worm, earth+berry — using the picture clues in the textbook. Teacher circulates and prompts students to say each compound word aloud before writing it.

Whole-class check: teacher invites volunteers to say and spell each compound word aloud while the rest of the class confirms. Teacher closes by asking if anyone can think of another compound word they know, encouraging one or two spontaneous contributions.

periods.teacher_notes: The compound-word task rewards students who notice that 'bluebell' and 'blueberry' are also possibilities — affirm creative thinking while confirming the textbook pairings. 'Earthworm' and 'basketball' are the two most common mix-ups when students swap the friend-word column; a quick 'does that picture match?' prompt is usually enough to self-correct.

items.source_lo: Student reads and answers literal and inferential questions using a short sharing-themed poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two-stanza crayon-sharing poem; colour words; contrast of 'you have' and 'I have'; full pack.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 4 beginning "I need the red". Which of the following best explains why the two children decide to share their crayons?

options.label: A
options.text: Each child has some colours the other does not, so together they have a full set.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither child likes their own crayons.

options.label: C
options.text: One child has no crayons at all.

options.label: D
options.text: The children want to paint a picture of a rainbow.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has not read the poem carefully and invented a reason not stated in the text.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has misread the contrast — the poem says each child has some crayons, not none.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has brought in outside knowledge about colour-mixing rather than reading the poem's own logic.

items.source_lo: Student reads and answers literal and inferential questions using a short sharing-themed poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two-stanza crayon-sharing poem; colour words; contrast of 'you have' and 'I have'; full pack.
items.item_stem: In the poem, one child says "I need the red and you need the black." Why does having different needs make sharing a good idea? Write your answer in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sharing is a good idea because each child needs what the other already has, so when they combine their crayons nobody is missing a colour and both children can use a full pack.

items.source_lo: Student speaks about personal experience and engages in guided conversation using a poem's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sharing crayons; colour names; paired talk about drawing; colour-ink naming challenge.
items.item_stem: Look at page 7 in your textbook where colour words are printed in different ink colours. Your teacher will point to each word. Listen carefully — is the reader saying the colour of the ink or the colour the word spells? Judge each word: True if the reader says the ink colour, False if the reader says the written word.

options.text: The reader says BLACK when pointing to the word RED printed in black ink.
The reader says GREEN when pointing to the word YELLOW printed in green ink.
The reader says ORANGE when pointing to the word BLUE printed in orange ink.
The reader says PURPLE when pointing to the word PURPLE printed in blue ink.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True (saying the ink colour GREEN is correct). 2 — True (saying the ink colour BLACK is correct). 3 — True (saying the ink colour ORANGE is correct). 4 — False (the ink colour is blue, so the reader should say BLUE, not PURPLE).

items.item_stem: The children in the poem share their crayons so that together they have all the colours they need. Think of something you share with a friend at school. Tell the class: what you share, who you share it with, and why sharing makes things better.

expected_elements: Names a specific item shared with a friend.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: blue + bell = bluebell, basket + ball = basketball, earth + worm = earthworm, straw + berry = strawberry.

items.item_stem: The textbook says words have friends, just like people do. Think of one compound word you know — a word made of two smaller words joined together. Tell the class both the smaller words and the new compound word they make.

expected_elements: Names two separate smaller words clearly.
Correctly combines them into a compound word.
Compound word is a real English word.
